analysis.one_liner: Requires rear, side, and front underride guards on large trucks and trailers so cars can't slide underneath in a crash.
analysis.headline: The Stop Underrides Act of 2017, introduced with bipartisan sponsorship, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When a car crashes into a large truck or trailer, the car can slide underneath, and the truck's body shears through the windshield and passenger compartment. The bill would order the Department of Transportation to write rules requiring strong rear, side, and front underride guards on trucks and trailers over 10,000 pounds, plus retrofits for older trailers and a system of inspections to keep the guards in working order. It responds to crash-test standards and research the National Transportation Safety Board had recommended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drives or rides in a passenger car. The bill's findings cite National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports of hundreds of preventable fatalities and life-threatening injuries from underride crashes, and it names dozens of victims. Drivers and their families gain a legally enforceable standard that the car they are in stops before going under a truck. Insurers of passenger vehicles and crash victims also stand to gain from fewer catastrophic claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Passenger car drivers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires DOT to issue rules mandating rear underride guards on all trailers, semi-trailers, and single unit trucks over 10,000 pounds, tested to stop a 35 mph passenger car from sliding underneath in center, 50%, and 30% overlap impacts [S3].

Requires side underride guards that stop intrusion into the passenger compartment from impacts at angles between 10 and 90 degrees, and front underride guards on commercial motor vehicles, with retrofit rules for trucks and trailers already on the road [S3].

Requires periodic, post-crash, and pre-trip inspections of underride guards, with fines and out-of-service orders for vehicles with rusted, cracked, or damaged guards, so the protection actually works years after installation [S3].

Directs DOT to publish quarterly data on underride crash victims on a public website and to develop prototypes protecting against crashes at up to 65 mph, with five-year reviews to keep standards current [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Truck and trailer manufacturers, which must design, test, and install three types of guards on new equipment, and motor carriers, which must retrofit existing trailers, pay fines for damaged guards, and absorb inspection downtime. Those costs would likely be passed into freight prices, touching shipping costs for businesses and consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Truck, trailer makers and freight carriers

drawbacks.text: The retrofit rules apply to trailers and trucks already in service, within 1 to 3 years depending on the guard type, which is the costliest provision for fleet owners and small carriers holding older equipment [S3].
Guards add weight and cost to every trailer, and the inspection regime adds downtime and repair expense for carriers; those costs flow through freight rates [S3].

Supporters of the existing weaker rear-guard standard argued that stronger requirements and side guards needed more cost-benefit analysis; DOT itself did not mandate side guards after the NTSB recommendation, an objection honest supporters of this bill would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is concrete: hundreds of preventable deaths and life-changing injuries per the NHTSA figures cited in the findings, most of them to people in cars doing nothing wrong. The costs are real but ordinary for motor-vehicle safety regulation — equipment, retrofit, and inspection costs spread across the freight economy. The bill gives DOT phase-in flexibility of up to 2-3 years, which softens the burden on existing fleets. On balance, the design is a fairly standard, workable safety mandate whose main obstacle was never its engineering but the absence of any committee action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 without a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill on December 12, 2017, joined by Sens. Marco Rubio (R-FL) and Bill Nelson (D-FL), giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that was the final action of its entire history [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored — six Democrats and one Republican — but the committee held no hearing or markup and the bill never reached the floor before Congress adjourned [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Truck and trailer manufacturers and freight carriers avoided new guard, retrofit, and inspection costs, while the families of underride crash victims got no new protection. Everyone who drives near trucks continued to face the same underride risk.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — a Democrat lead sponsor with a Republican (Rubio) and Democrat (Nelson) as original cosponsors, and 6 of 7 later cosponsors were Democrats — but there was no vote on which to measure broader party positions.

industries.note: The bill requires them to design, crash-test, and install rear, side, and front underride guards on all large trucks and trailers, and to retrofit older equipment within 1 to 3 years. Their cost of compliance is the cost of the protection that car occupants would gain.

Carriers face retrofit costs, fines and out-of-service orders for damaged guards, and added pre-trip, periodic, and post-crash inspection downtime. Freight rates would carry some of that cost, but the bill's core beneficiary is the people in the cars that hit the trailers.
